newsitem.title: USA: U.S. refiners may get taste of Iraqi Kirkuk crude.
newsitem.headline: U.S. refiners may get taste of Iraqi Kirkuk crude.

text.p: A change in the price structure for Iraqi Kirkuk crude oil has raised the prospect of shipments to the U.S. for the first time since before Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990, traders said.

During the December-to-June round of the U.N. "oil-for-food" program, prices for both Basrah Light and Kirkuk crude were based off of the second-month quote for U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing (WTI).
Because of differences in transportation costs, this price structure rendered Kirkuk uneconomic to deliver into the U.S. Gulf Coast, traders said.

Under the new price structure Kirkuk is linked to front-month WTI, which currently is about 20 cents per barrel lower than the second month (October) contract and means it is favorable for U.S. buyers.
Kirkuk crude is shipped out of the Turkish port of Ceyhan in the Mediterranean, from where it takes an estimated 22-25 days to reach the U.S. Gulf Coast.
In contrast, Basrah is shipped out of the Iraqi port of Mina al-Bakr in the Mideast Gulf, from where it takes about 40-45 days to reach the U.S. Gulf.
Traders said potential sellers were currently showing Kirkuk at $1.70-1.80 a barrel under October WTI for mid-September delivery into the U.S. Gulf on a cif basis.
Basrah was being indicated at $1.90-2.00 under November WTI for early October arrival in the U.S. Gulf.
"We haven't run (Kirkuk), but we're anxious for someone to bring it over so we can run an assay on it," said a trader for a U.S. refiner in the Southwest.
Kirkuk is a light sour grade that would compete with other sour crudes from regional producers such as Venezuela, traders said.

Since the war the crudes have gotten slightly heavier, traders said. Kirkuk is now assessed at 35.9 degrees American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity and 1.95 percent sulfur. Before the war, it tested at an API gravity of 37 degrees and a sulfur content of two percent.
Basrah is now seen at 33 to 33.5 degrees API with two percent sulfur compared to pre-war measurements of 34.4 degrees API with 2.1 percent sulfur.
Under the U.N. oil-for-food deal, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months for humanitarian needs as an exception to sanctions imposed in 1990.
The second round is set to begin imminently after the U.N. gave the green light to Iraq's oil price formula on Friday.
